parts: Please read the results in /shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/prime-variance-exponents/notes/programs/01_signed_arithmetic_covariance/FINITE_CROSS_SPECTRUM_20261004.md and previous notes, and tell me your overall assessment of the progress
I’ll read the latest result and the preceding notes, then assess what has been established, how it fits the larger program, and what remains unresolved.

The latest note does remove a whole frequency range at the required error scale. The central signed correlation is still open. I’m checking whether the preceding reductions make that correlation easier to estimate, and whether the failed shortcuts reveal a common obstruction.

The strongest progress is clearer now: the scalar criterion removes the need for a separate global energy estimate, density centering cancels the full continuum, and the tail bound leaves a precisely defined central target. The mode calculations also show why multiplying two arithmetic errors does not automatically improve decay: their coupling preserves the original hypothetical zero contribution. That makes the next missing estimate more specific.

**The program has made substantial progress in isolating the arithmetic problem and controlling its errors. It remains at the reduction stage: the first fixed global power saving is still open, and no successful mechanism for producing it has yet emerged.**

After reading the latest note, its companion attempts, and the preceding Möbius/Vaughan, Mellin, and scalar investigations, three advances stand out.

- **The scalar criterion genuinely simplifies the task.** Either one-sided bound for the complete centered scalar suffices globally; a separate projected-energy theorem is unnecessary. This removes a substantial obligation from the earlier plan. Its strength remains exactly that of the desired zero-strip result, so the simplification concerns what must be estimated, not the underlying arithmetic difficulty. [Scalar continuation](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/prime-variance-exponents/notes/programs/01_signed_arithmetic_covariance/SIGNED_COVARIANCE_CONTINUATION_20261004.md:49).

- **The density cancellation and arithmetic localization are concrete results.** The continuum cancels before requiring a separate estimate for the reciprocal Möbius sum. Lattice and boundary terms receive explicit power budgets, and the aggregated kernel permits deletion of a divisor range at the target error scale. These calculations actually bound discarded contributions. [Density cancellation](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/prime-variance-exponents/notes/programs/01_signed_arithmetic_covariance/ONE_SIDED_ARITHMETIC_ATTEMPT_20261004.md:50), [aggregated kernel](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/prime-variance-exponents/notes/programs/01_signed_arithmetic_covariance/AGGREGATED_KERNEL_CONTINUATION_20261004.md).

- **The finite cross-spectrum note adds a useful unconditional lemma.** In its notation,
  \[
  Q=\mathcal C_T(X)+O(X^{-\kappa/2}),\qquad
  T=X^{\kappa/14}[\log(2X)]^{4/7}.
  \]
  The entire discarded frequency range is paid for using elementary estimates, without assuming stronger Möbius or prime cancellation. I found no substantive problem in the normalization, density correction, mean-square argument, or logarithmic budget. This is the clearest new achievement of the latest continuation. [Finite spectral reduction](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/prime-variance-exponents/notes/programs/01_signed_arithmetic_covariance/FINITE_CROSS_SPECTRUM_20261004.md:118).

The central limitation is now especially clear. **Finite bandwidth does not remove the coherent arithmetic contribution.** The bandwidth grows with \(X\), so every fixed frequency eventually remains inside it. The multiplier is nonzero at zero, and frequency separation supplies only logarithmic improvement in the displayed mode test.

More decisively, the mixed-discrepancy and arithmetic-closure calculations show that matching hypothetical zero modes reproduce the original coefficient, including arbitrary multiplicities and an affordable boundary remainder. Consequently, the appearance of two arithmetic errors supplies no automatic improvement in decay. This is a valuable diagnostic, carefully distinguished from an expansion of the actual errors into zeros. [Mode calculation](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/prime-variance-exponents/notes/programs/01_signed_arithmetic_covariance/ARITHMETIC_CLOSURE_ATTEMPT_20261004.md:274).

I also regard the negative results as meaningful progress. Separate semiprime-sector bounds fail on actual arithmetic coefficients; literal sign deletion loses indispensable cancellation; and the proposed uncentered short-interval variance input would already imply a **stronger** zero-free strip than the intended target. These findings prevent plausible-looking arguments from quietly assuming the breakthrough they are supposed to deliver. [Dispersion audit](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/prime-variance-exponents/notes/programs/01_signed_arithmetic_covariance/SHORT_INTERVAL_DISPERSION_GATE_20261004.md:147). The cited short-interval uniformity results provide logarithmic savings for the relevant Möbius applications, leaving the fixed-power gap intact. [Primary source](https://arxiv.org/html/2204.03754v4).

My confidence is reasonably strong in these reductions after the present checks. The exact finite comparisons strengthen confidence in the algebra and endpoint handling; they provide no asymptotic evidence for the missing exponent. The reviews also remain internal same-model checks.

**I would continue program 01, with a stricter milestone now: a new quantitative inequality for the complete signed central correlation.** Further representations should earn their place by enabling that estimate, especially by addressing its coherent component. The illustrative \(\kappa=0.01\) would already give variance \(O(X^{2.99})\) and exclude zeros with real part above \(0.995\) at every height. That remains a major unresolved result.

The work has substantially sharpened our understanding of where a saving must come from. It has not yet demonstrated that the required cancellation is more accessible.

Is there any way that we could find an improved zero free region this way that isn't uniform? Is there a way to relate finite intervals to zero free regions, and improve on classical results that way? Finding any new zero free region would be very interesting
I’ll check how the variance bounds translate into regions that depend on height, and whether finite ranges could yield an improvement without requiring a fixed strip at every height.

See these two papers for recent significant results from Claude, if it can be improved on that would be very interesting I think [https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13637](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13637) and [https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02882](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02882)

I found two useful connections: published converse theorems turn prime-error bounds on finite intervals into zero exclusions, and your arithmetic-approximation notes already contain a finite-norm exclusion inequality. I’ll read the two papers you linked next to see what they improve and which parts might connect to this program.

The two papers concern proportions of zeros, so they address a different target from excluding every zero in a region. Lamzouri’s simpler proof looks useful here, but it also identifies a limit: changing the test window within that method cannot improve the 67.25% constant. A further gain would need additional arithmetic information or a different inequality.

**Yes. A region that depends on height—or an improvement confined to one height band—is a legitimate target without proving a fixed strip at every height.** The two papers also suggest another worthwhile target: improving the proportion of zeros proved simple and on the critical line.

I read their latest versions. The Alpöge–Furman paper attributes its discovery to Claude and obtains the \(67.25\%\) bound through a finite compression of Weil’s Hermitian form. Lamzouri gives a simpler Hilbert-space proof, recovers that bound, and adds further estimates. These are substantial proportion results, but they still permit isolated off-line zeros; they do not establish new zero-free regions. [Alpöge–Furman](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.13637v2), [Lamzouri](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.02882v2).

**There is a concrete finite-certificate connection already in your notes.** Program 06 constructs
\[
F_N(s)=\frac{1-\zeta(s)P_N(s)}s
      =\int_0^1 e_N(x)x^{s-1}\,dx.
\]
For \(0<b<\beta\), a zero \(\rho=\beta+i\gamma\) forces
\[
\mathcal E_b:=\int_0^1|e_N(x)|^2x^{2b-1}\,dx
\ \ge\ \frac{2(\beta-b)}{\beta^2+\gamma^2}.
\]
Consequently, **one finite certificate**
\[
\mathcal E_b<\frac{2(\beta_0-b)}{1+T^2}
\]
excludes every zero with \(\beta\ge\beta_0\) and \(|\gamma|\le T\). No convergence theorem or global variance improvement is required. The note supplies a finite-sum evaluation with an explicit remainder. [Arithmetic-approximation note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/prime-variance-exponents/notes/programs/06_arithmetic_approximation/PRELIMINARY_INVESTIGATION_20261004.md:90).

The difficulty is numerical strength: this unshifted certificate demands accuracy proportional to \(T^{-2}\). Height-localized test functions could improve sensitivity, but they require a more flexible approximation family.

Finite **prime intervals** also have a rigorous connection. Turán/Pintz-type converse theorems show that a hypothetical zero forces a sufficiently large prime-counting error somewhere in an explicitly specified finite interval. A certified error bound throughout that interval can therefore exclude the zero. Schlage-Puchta supplies such a theorem for \([X,X^{1+\varepsilon}]\), although its required starting scale is enormous. Applying this principle to our smoothed scalar would require a quantitative detection theorem accounting for cancellation between zeros. [Finite-interval converse](https://arxiv.org/html/1912.00853).

There is direct precedent for improving classical regions through a bounded range. Bellotti–Trudgian–Yang’s March 2026 paper proves
\[
\zeta(\sigma+it)\ne0
\quad\text{when}\quad
\sigma>1-\frac1{4.896\log|t|},\qquad |t|\ge3,
\]
by combining a finite-range improvement with an existing region above that range. Thus a useful local improvement can contribute to a theorem covering all heights. [Their theorem and finite-range argument](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.21490v1).

For improving the two papers you supplied, the obstacle is different. Lamzouri’s bound has the form
\[
\frac{N_{\mathrm{simple,on\ line}}}{N}\ge 2-A+o(1),
\qquad A=1.327499296\ldots.
\]
His Remark 3.4 establishes that changing the window within that method cannot lower this constant. A further gain needs additional arithmetic information, a larger class of admissible inequalities, or higher moments. Our signed covariance work might help supply the missing prime-correlation information, but we have not derived that connection. [Lamzouri’s optimality statement](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.02882v2#S3).

I would therefore pursue two focused targets:

- **For a new zero-free region:** a certificate for one specified height band, with its boundary compared against the strongest existing region there. A band above the verified critical-line range—approximately \(3\times10^{12}\)—would be meaningful. [Existing verification](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.09765).
- **For improving \(67.25\%\):** derive the exact prime-correlation estimate needed beyond the presently controlled Fourier-support range, then test whether our signed arithmetic identities help estimate it. That support parameter is distinct from the frequency cutoff in the finite cross-spectrum note.

These are useful intermediate goals. Neither requires first solving the fixed-strip problem, and either would count as mathematical progress. We have concrete routes to investigate, but no improved region or proportion has yet been established by our work.

I’m using the write-page skill to record the findings in the investigation’s notes folder. I’m checking that benchmark first: otherwise we could mistake a consequence of known zero-free regions for new arithmetic progress.

The cutoff and tail estimates already accommodate such an envelope. What remains is to distinguish a stronger bound supplied by classical smoothing from cancellation that would actually exclude additional zeros.

I now have a checked improvement to the project’s unconditional baseline, derived from existing zero-free regions and zero-density estimates. It roughly doubles the exponential decay coefficient in the stated variance bound, though it excludes no additional zeros. This gives us a much better benchmark for judging future arithmetic estimates. I’m also checking whether adapting the probe to a chosen height would make local exclusion more feasible.

The height-adapted probe passes the algebraic checks and gives a concrete improvement in detection: its coefficient at the chosen zero height stays above \(0.36\) on a right substrip, while the fixed probe’s coefficient decays like height to the power minus seven. This looks better suited to a local zero-free result. It still needs a quantitative argument controlling nearby-zero cancellation and a corresponding arithmetic bound.

**The most natural direction is a height-dependent bound for the complete signed, smoothed prime sum, coupled to a quantitative zero detector.** The investigation produced three useful findings.

1. **The classical benchmark is stronger than our notes currently state.** Using existing zero-free regions, classical zero-density estimates, and our probe’s smoothing, I derived
   \[
   \mathcal V_g(X)\ll_\varepsilon
   X^3e^{-(0.870585-\varepsilon)F(X)},\qquad
   F(X)=\frac{(\log X)^{3/5}}{(\log\log X)^{1/5}}.
   \]
   The manuscript’s current exponential coefficient is \(0.3706\). This substantially improves our asymptotic baseline, but comes entirely from established zero information; it excludes no additional zeros. The derivation uses [Bellotti’s region](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.10680) and [classical density estimates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15184).

2. **Our arithmetic reduction already supports nonuniform envelopes.** We can replace the fixed-power target by \(e^{-\Phi(\log X)}\), with \(\Phi\to\infty\) and \(\Phi=o(\log X)\), and pay all existing comparison and spectral-tail errors. Thus the machinery does not force us to seek a uniform strip. However, the existing Landau argument does not convert such an envelope into a curved zero-free region.

3. **Adapting the probe to height substantially improves detection.** I constructed a prepared probe centered at height \(t\), together with a matching shell average. Its coefficient at \(\beta+it\) exceeds \(0.36\) for \(3/4\le\beta\le1\), \(|t|\ge100\), with an exact algebraic proof. The fixed probe’s coefficient instead decays like \(|t|^{-7}\). The price is growing derivative constants and a complex arithmetic scalar.

**My assessment is that the strongest next direction is the interface between this height-adapted detector and the complete signed arithmetic correlation.** A quantitative theorem giving a detection interval, including nearby-zero cancellation, would be a concrete advance. An independently proved arithmetic bound on that interval could then support a local zero-free improvement. Neither step is complete, so there is not yet evidence sufficient to predict a new region.

The [Alpöge–Furman](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13637) and [Lamzouri](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02882) proportion results require a different, height-averaged prime-pair bound. Our present product correlation has no established bridge to that bound; simple window optimization is already exhausted within their existing quadratic family.
